**Surah al-Hashr**
It has twenty-four verses and is Medinan.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah, and He is the Almighty, the All-Wise.﴾ ﴿It is He who expelled those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture from their homes at the first gathering.﴾

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah, and He is the Almighty, the All-Wise.﴾ ﴿It is He who expelled those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture from their homes at the first gathering.﴾ The Banu al-Nadir made a treaty with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that they would neither be against him nor be with anyone against him. When he prevailed at the Battle of Badr, they said: "This is the Prophet described in the Torah as the one who will be given victory." But when the Muslims were defeated at the Battle of Uhud, they doubted and broke their covenant. Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf set out with forty riders to Makkah and made an alliance with Abu Sufyan at the Ka'bah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then ordered Muhammad ibn Maslamah al-Ansari, and he killed Ka'b by treachery; Ka'b was his foster brother. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) marched against them with the battalions, while he was riding a donkey with a halter of palm fiber. He said to them: "Leave the city." They replied: "Death is dearer to us than that." Then they called out for war. It is also said that they asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for a delay of ten days to prepare for departure. He sent Abdullah ibn Ubayy to them, and he said: "Do not leave the fortress. If they fight you, we are with you and will not abandon you. And if you leave, we will certainly leave with you." So they fortified the alleys, and he besieged them for twenty-one nights. When Allah cast terror into their hearts and they despaired of the support of the hypocrites, they asked for peace. He refused anything but exile, on the condition that each three of them could carry on one camel whatever goods they wished. So they departed to Syria, to Ariha and Adhruat. Only two households, among them the family of Abu al-Haqiq and the family of Huyayy ibn Akhtab, went to Khaybar, and a group went to al-Hirah. And here there are questions.

The first question: What is the meaning of this lam in His saying: ﴿for the first gathering﴾ (*li-awwali al-hashr*)?

The answer: It is the lam like in your saying: "I came at the time of such-and-such," and the meaning is: He expelled those who disbelieved at the first gathering.

The second question: What is the meaning of "the first gathering" (*awwal al-hashr*)?

The answer: *Al-hashr* is the bringing out of a group from one place to another. As for why this gathering is called "the first gathering," its explanation is according to several aspects:

The first, which is the view of Ibn Abbas and most scholars, is that this was the first gathering and expulsion of the People of the Scripture from the Arabian Peninsula, and this humiliation had not befallen them before, because they had been a people of strength and honor.

The second: He, exalted is He, made their expulsion from Medina a gathering, and made it the first gathering because people will be gathered for the Hour toward the region of Syria, and then the Hour will overtake them there.

The third: This is the first of their gatherings, and as for their last gathering, it is the exile that Umar carried out against them from Khaybar to Syria.

The fourth: Its meaning is that He expelled them from their homes at the first time He gathered them for fighting, because it was the first battle that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) fought against them.

The fifth: Qatadah said: "This is the first gathering, and the second gathering is a fire that will gather people from the east to the west. It will spend the night with them wherever they spend the night, and it will rest with them wherever they rest." They also mentioned that this fire is seen at night and is not seen during the day.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 59, verse 2:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Little did you think that they would go forth﴾.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: The Muslims thought that, because of their might and strength, they had no need to go forth from their homes. God, exalted is He, mentioned this to magnify this blessing, for a blessing is greater when it arrives while one's expectation is otherwise. The Muslims had not thought they would attain their aim of seeing these Jews depart, so that they would be freed from the harm of their schemes. When this was made easy for them, the anticipation of this blessing was greater.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they thought that their fortresses would defend them from God﴾.

They said: Their fortresses were impregnable, so they thought that these would protect them from the Messenger of God. The verse contains a great honour for the Messenger of God, for it indicates that dealing with them through the Messenger of God is the very same as dealing with God. If it is said: What is the difference between your saying "they thought that their fortresses would defend them" or "their fortresses were defending them," and the structure in which it came? We say: In placing the predicate before the subject there is evidence of the extreme confidence they placed in the fortresses' protection and defence of them; and in making their pronoun the subject and attributing the clause to it, there is evidence of their belief in themselves that they were in might and defence, caring not for anyone who might covet contending with them. These meanings do not arise in your saying: "and they thought that their fortresses would defend them."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then God came upon them from where they did not expect﴾. On this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: The verse has two interpretations.

The first: that the pronoun in His saying ﴿came upon them﴾ refers to the Jews, meaning that God's punishment came upon them and seized them from where they did not expect.

The second: that it refers to the believers, meaning that God's help and strengthening came to them from where they did not expect. The meaning of "did not expect" is that they did not suppose it and it did not occur to them. This was due to two matters:

One of them: the killing of their chief, Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf, at the hand of his brother by treachery, which weakened their strength, broke their arm, and diminished their power.

The second: what He cast into their hearts of terror.

The second issue: His saying ﴿Then God came upon them﴾ cannot be taken in its apparent sense by the agreement of the majority of rational people, and this indicates that the door of interpretation (taʾwil) is open, and that turning verses away from their apparent meanings in accordance with rational proofs is permissible.

The third issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: it has been read "fa-ataahumu Allah" (so God brought it to them), meaning "so destruction came to them." Know that this reading does not dispel what we have explained of the aspects of interpretation, because this reading does not displace the first reading, which is established by mass transmission (tawatur); and whenever a reading is established by tawatur it cannot be dismissed, rather interpretation is necessary in it.

* *

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He cast terror into their hearts﴾. The lexicographers said: ar-Ruʿb (terror) is the fear that fills the breast, that is, fills it up; and its "qadhf" (casting) is placing it within. Concerning this they said of the lion: muqadhdhaf (cast-filled), as if it had been flung with flesh, due to its compactness and the interlocking of its parts. Know that this verse indicates our view that all affairs belong to God, because the verse shows that the occurrence of that terror in their hearts was from God, and it shows that that terror became a cause for their undertaking certain acts. In sum, an act does not come about except when a strong motive arises in the heart, and the arising of that motive is not except from God; thus all acts are ascribed to God in this way.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They ruined their houses with their own hands and the hands of the believers﴾. On this there are issues:

The first issue: Abu ʿAli said: Abu ʿAmr alone read "yukhharribuna" with shadda (doubled rāʾ), while the others read "yukhribuna" without it. Abu ʿAmr used to say: al-ikhrab is that a thing be left in ruin, and at-takhrib is demolition, and the Banu al-Nadir were "kharribu" (ruined/demolished) and were not "ukhribu". Al-Mubarrad said: I do not know a basis for this; "yukhribuna" is the original form: khariba al-manzil and akhrabahu its owner, like ʿalima and aʿlamahu, qama and aqamahu. When it is altered to "yukharribuna" from takhrib, it is for intensity, because He mentioned houses which are suitable for few and many. Sibawayh claimed that the two alternate in speech, so each takes the place of the other, like farrahtuhu and afrahtuhu, and hassanahu Allah and ahsanahu. Al-Aʿsha said:

"And I laid waste the homes of a people in their land"

Al-Farraʾ said: "yukharribuna" with doubling means they demolish, and with lightness "yukhribuna" means they leave them and abandon them.

The second issue: The exegetes mentioned several aspects in explaining how they ruined their houses with their own hands and the hands of the believers:

One of them: when they became certain of exile, they envied the Muslims settling in their dwellings and homes, so they began to ruin them from within, while the Muslims did so from without.

The second: Muqatil said: the hypocrites secretly urged them not to leave, and they fortified the alleys; so they tore down their houses and made them like fortresses at the entrances of the alleys, while the Muslims ruined the remaining sides.

The third: when the Muslims gained the upper hand over one of their streets, they ruined it, and the Jews would retreat behind their houses and break through them from their rear.

The fourth: the Muslims were ruining the outskirts of the town, and the Jews, when they became certain of exile and were looking at the wood in their dwellings, which they found admirable, or the door, they demolished their houses and pulled them out and loaded them on camels. If it is said: what is the meaning of their ruin of them by the hands of the believers? We say: al-Zajjaj said: since they exposed them to that and were the cause of it, it is as if they had commanded them to it and assigned it to them.

* *

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So take warning, O you with insight﴾.

Know that we have relied on this verse in our book "al-Mahsul min Usul al-Fiqh" to establish that analogy (qiyas) is a proof, so we will not mention it here; however, it is necessary here to explain the aspect for which God commanded taking warning (iʿtibar), and there are possibilities:

One: They relied on their fortresses, their strength and their might, so God destroyed their might and removed their power, then said: ﴿So take warning, O you with insight﴾, and do not rely on anything other than God. The ascetic has no right to rely on his asceticism, for his asceticism is no more than the asceticism of Balʿam; and the scholar has no right to rely on his knowledge: look at Ibn al-Rawandi despite his great study, how he turned out. Rather, no one relies on anything except the bounty and mercy of God.

Two: The judge (al-Qadi) said: the intended meaning is that a person should know the consequence of treachery, disbelief, and slander against prophethood, for those Jews fell, by the evil of treachery and disbelief, into affliction and exile, and believers also take warning from it and turn away from sins.

If it is said: this warning is valid only if we say that they betrayed and disbelieved and were punished, and the cause of that punishment was disbelief and treachery; but this claim is invalid both in its inclusion and its exclusion. As for inclusion: many a person has betrayed and disbelieved and was not punished in this world. As for exclusion: similar trials, indeed harsher, befell the Messenger, peace be upon him, and his companions, and this did not indicate the corruption of their religion or their deeds. When this cause is invalid, this warning is also invalid. Furthermore, the third term in the original case is that ﴿they ruined their houses with their own hands and the hands of the believers﴾; and if we ascribe that to disbelief and treachery, it would follow that everyone who betrays and disbelieves should ruin his house with his own hand and the hands of the Muslims, and it is known that this is not appropriate; so we know that this warning is not valid.

The answer: The established ruling in the original case has three levels:

The first: that it is the ruin of the house by their hands and the hands of the believers.

The second, which is more general than the first: that it is punishment in this world.

The third, which is more general than the second: that it is punishment in general. Betrayal and disbelief are appropriate to punishment insofar as it is punishment; as for the particular quality of it being demolition or killing in this world or in the Hereafter, that has no effect. So the result of the analogy returns to: those who betrayed, disbelieved and denied were punished, without regard to whether that punishment was in this world or the Hereafter.

Betrayal and disbelief are appropriate to punishment, so we know that disbelief and treachery are the two causes of punishment; wherever they occur, punishment occurs, without specifying whether that punishment is in this world or the Hereafter. When we establish the analogy and the warning on this basis, the objections and counter-examples fall away, and the analogy is completed in its correct form.

The second issue: iʿtibar is derived from crossing over and passing beyond something; for this reason a tear is called ʿibrah, because it moves from the eye to the cheek; a ford is called maʿbar because through it crossing is achieved; the science of dream interpretation is called taʿbir, because its practitioner moves from the imagined to the intelligible; and words are called ʿibarat, because they convey meanings from the speaker's tongue to the listener's mind. It is said: the happy one is he who takes warning from others, because his mind moves from the state of that other to the state of himself. For this reason the exegetes said: iʿtibar is reflection upon the realities of things and the aspects of their indication, so that through reflecting upon them something else of their kind may be known.

As for His saying ﴿O you with insight﴾, there are two interpretations:

The first: Ibn ʿAbbas said: He means O people of intellect, reason and insight.

The second: al-Farraʾ said: ﴿O you with insight﴾ means O you who witnessed that event mentioned.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 59, verses 3–4:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And had it not been that Allah had decreed for them exile, He would have punished them in this world; and for them in the Hereafter is the punishment of the Fire.﴾ The meaning of al-jala' (exile) in the lexicon is departing from one's homeland and moving away from it. If it is said: "law la" (had it not been) indicates the negation of one thing because of the existence of another, so from the existence of exile it follows that there is no punishment in this world; but exile is a kind of punishment, so from the existence of exile it follows that it does not exist, and this is impossible. We say: its meaning is: "And had it not been that Allah had decreed for them exile, He would have punished them in this world by killing, as was done to their brothers, Banu Qurayzah." As for His saying: ﴿and for them in the Hereafter is the punishment of the Fire⌋, it is an independent statement and not conjoined to what precedes it, for if it were conjoined to what precedes it, it would follow that it would not exist, because of what we have explained, that law la (had it not been) requires the negation of the consequent due to the occurrence of the condition.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is because they opposed Allah and His Messenger﴾, it indicates that the cause of that destruction is opposing Allah and His Messenger. If it is said: if opposition were the cause of this destruction, it would necessarily be said that wherever this opposition occurs, destruction occurs, and it is known that this is not so. We say: this is one of the things that shows that the specification of a explicitly stated cause does not invalidate its soundness.

Then He said: ﴿And whoever opposes Allah—indeed, Allah is severe in punishment﴾, and the purpose of it is deterrence.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 59, verses 5–6:**

God Most High says: ﴿Whatever palm trees you cut down, or left standing on their roots, was by the permission of God, and so that He might disgrace the defiantly disobedient.﴾ Concerning this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** ﴿min līnatin﴾ (of palm trees) explains what ﴿mā qaṭa'tum﴾ (whatever you cut down) refers to. The place of ﴿mā﴾ is in the accusative, governed by ﴿qaṭa'tum﴾ (you cut down), as if he said: "What thing did you cut down?" The pronoun referring back to ﴿mā﴾ in His words ﴿aw taraktumūhā﴾ (or left it) is feminine, because ﴿mā﴾ here means ﴿al-līnah﴾ (the palm tree).

**The second issue:** Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-līnah is the palm tree, as long as it is not an ʿajwah or a barniyyah (two kinds of dates). The original form of līnah is lawnah, and the wāw was dropped because of the kasrah on the lām. Its plural is alwān. It refers to all palm trees except the barniyy and the ʿajwah. Some scholars said: al-līnah is the noble palm tree, as if they derived it from al-līn (softness/tenderness), and its plural is līn. If it is asked: Why was al-līnah specifically singled out for cutting? We answer: If it is from the alwān (varieties), then let them keep for themselves the ʿajwah and the barniyyah; and if it is from the noble palms, then the rage of the Jews would be greater.

**The third issue:** The author of al-Kashshaf said: It was recited as ﴿qawmān ʿalā uṣulihā﴾. In this there are two possibilities:

One of them: it is the plural of aṣl (root), like rahn and ruhun (pledge and pledges), where the ḍammah is sufficient instead of the wāw. It was also recited as ﴿qā'iman ʿalā uṣūlihi﴾, going back to the wording of ﴿mā﴾. As for His words ﴿fa-bi-idhni llāh﴾ (then by the permission of God), it means: their cutting was by the permission and command of God. ﴿Wa-li-yukhziya al-fāsiqīn﴾ means: and for the purpose of disgracing the defiantly disobedient, that is, the Jews; God permitted their cutting down.

**The fourth issue:** It is reported that when the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered that their palm trees be cut down and burned, they said: "O Muhammad, you used to forbid corruption on the earth, so what is this cutting of palm trees and burning them?" Some of the believers had some feeling about this, and so this verse was revealed. The meaning is that God permitted this only so that the rage of the disbelievers would increase, and their grief would be doubled by the execution of the ruling of their enemies over their most prized possessions.

**The fifth issue:** Scholars have used this verse as evidence that it is permissible to demolish, burn, flood, and bombard with catapults the fortresses and dwellings of the disbelievers. Likewise, it is permissible to uproot their trees, whether they bear fruit or not. It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud: "They cut from them only what was a place for fighting."

**The sixth issue:** It is reported that two men were cutting palm trees, one of them cutting the ʿajwah and the other the lawn. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) asked them. This one said: "I left it for the Messenger of God." And that one said: "I cut it to enrage the disbelievers." They used this as evidence for the permissibility of ijtihad (independent reasoning), and for its permissibility in the presence of the Messenger.

God Most High says: ﴿And whatever God restored to His Messenger from them, you did not spur any horse or camel toward it, but God gives authority to His messengers over whomever He wills, and God is over all things capable.﴾

Al-Mubarrad said: It is said: fā'a yafī'u, when he returned; and afā'ahu Allah, when God returned it. Al-Azhari said: al-fay' (the spoils of return) is what God restores to the people of His religion from the property of those who opposed the people of His religion without fighting, either by their being exiled from their homelands and leaving them to the Muslims, or by reconciling with them on a jizyah (poll tax) that they pay for their heads, or on property other than the jizyah with which they ransom themselves from the shedding of their blood, as the Banu al-Nadir did when they reconciled with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on the condition that for every three of them, a camel's load of whatever they chose would be taken, except weapons, and they would leave the rest. This property is the fay', and it is what God restored to the Muslims, that is, He returned it from the disbelievers to the Muslims. His words ﴿minhum﴾ (from them) means from the Jews of Banu al-Nadir. His words ﴿fa-mā awjaftum﴾ (you did not spur): it is said: wajafa al-faras wal-ba'ir yajifu wajfan wa-wajīfan, meaning rapid travel; and awjafahu ṣāḥibuhu means when its rider drove it to rapid travel. His words ﴿ʿalayhi﴾ (toward it) means toward what God restored. His words ﴿min khayl wa-lā rikāb﴾ (any horse or camel): al-rikāb is what is ridden of camels, whose singular is rāḥilah, and it has no singular from its own form. The Arabs do not apply the word rākib (rider) except to the rider of a camel, and they call the rider of a horse fāris (horseman).

The meaning of the verse is that the Companions asked the Messenger (ʿalayhi al-ṣalāt wal-salām) to divide the fay' among them just as he divided the ghanimah (war booty) among them. So God mentioned the difference between the two matters: the ghanimah is what you exerted yourselves to obtain, spurring horses and camels toward it, unlike the fay', for you did not undergo any hardship in obtaining it. Therefore the matter concerning it was entrusted to the Messenger, who places it wherever he wills.

Then here there is a question: The property of the Banu al-Nadir was taken after fighting, because they were besieged for days, and they fought, and were killed, then they reconciled on exile. Therefore that property should be part of the ghanimah, not part of the fay'. Because of this question, the commentators mention here two answers:

The first: This verse was not revealed concerning the villages of the Banu al-Nadir, because they were not spurred toward with horses and camels, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the Muslims did not besiege them. Rather, it concerns Fadak, because the people of Fadak withdrew from it, so those villages and property came into the hand of the Messenger (ʿalayhi al-salām) without war. The Messenger (ʿalayhi al-ṣalāt wal-salām) used to take from the income of Fadak his own sustenance and the sustenance of those he supported, and he put the remainder into weapons and horses. When he died, Fatimah (ʿalayha al-salām) claimed that he had granted Fadak to her. Abu Bakr said: "You are the most dear of people to me in poverty and the most beloved to me in wealth, but I do not know the validity of your claim, and it is not permissible for me to rule on that." Then Umm Ayman and a freedman of the Messenger (ʿalayhi al-salām) bore witness for her. Abu Bakr asked her for the witness whose testimony is acceptable in the Sharia, and there was none. So Abu Bakr applied to it what the Messenger (ﷺ) used to apply: he spent from it on those whom the Messenger used to support, and he put what remained into weapons and horses. Likewise 'Umar placed it in the hand of 'Ali to administer it in this manner, and at the end of 'Umar's time he returned it to 'Umar, and said: "We have sufficiency, and the Muslims have need of it." 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him) administered it in the same way, then it passed to 'Ali, and he administered it in this manner. So the four imams agreed upon this.

The second opinion: This verse was revealed concerning the Banu al-Nadir and their villages. The Muslims at that time did not have many horses or camels, and they had not traveled a great distance to them. They were only two miles from Medina, so they walked to them on foot, and none rode except the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who was riding a camel. When the fighting force was small, and the horses and riding camels were not available, God the Exalted treated them as what no fighting force had been involved in at all. So God singled out the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for those properties. Then it is reported that he divided them among the Emigrants, and he gave none of them to the Helpers except three men who were in need: Abu Dujanah, Sahl ibn Hunayf, and al-Harith ibn al-Simmah.

**The sixth issue:** It is reported that two men were cutting palm trees, one of them cutting the ʿajwah and the other the lawn. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) asked them. This one said: "I left it for the Messenger of God." And that one said: "I cut it to enrage the disbelievers." They used this as evidence for the permissibility of ijtihad (independent reasoning), and for its permissibility in the presence of the Messenger.

God Most High says: ﴿And whatever God restored to His Messenger from them, you did not spur any horse or camel toward it, but God gives authority to His messengers over whomever He wills, and God is over all things capable.﴾

Al-Mubarrad said: It is said: fā'a yafī'u, when he returned; and afā'ahu Allah, when God returned it. Al-Azhari said: al-fay' (the spoils of return) is what God restores to the people of His religion from the property of those who opposed the people of His religion without fighting, either by their being exiled from their homelands and leaving them to the Muslims, or by reconciling with them on a jizyah (poll tax) that they pay for their heads, or on property other than the jizyah with which they ransom themselves from the shedding of their blood, as the Banu al-Nadir did when they reconciled with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on the condition that for every three of them, a camel's load of whatever they chose would be taken, except weapons, and they would leave the rest. This property is the fay', and it is what God restored to the Muslims, that is, He returned it from the disbelievers to the Muslims. His words ﴿minhum﴾ (from them) means from the Jews of Banu al-Nadir. His words ﴿fa-mā awjaftum﴾ (you did not spur): it is said: wajafa al-faras wal-ba'ir yajifu wajfan wa-wajīfan, meaning rapid travel; and awjafahu ṣāḥibuhu means when its rider drove it to rapid travel. His words ﴿ʿalayhi﴾ (toward it) means toward what God restored. His words ﴿min khayl wa-lā rikāb﴾ (any horse or camel): al-rikāb is what is ridden of camels, whose singular is rāḥilah, and it has no singular from its own form. The Arabs do not apply the word rākib (rider) except to the rider of a camel, and they call the rider of a horse fāris (horseman).

The meaning of the verse is that the Companions asked the Messenger (ʿalayhi al-ṣalāt wal-salām) to divide the fay' among them just as he divided the ghanimah (war booty) among them. So God mentioned the difference between the two matters: the ghanimah is what you exerted yourselves to obtain, spurring horses and camels toward it, unlike the fay', for you did not undergo any hardship in obtaining it. Therefore the matter concerning it was entrusted to the Messenger, who places it wherever he wills.

Then here there is a question: The property of the Banu al-Nadir was taken after fighting, because they were besieged for days, and they fought, and were killed, then they reconciled on exile. Therefore that property should be part of the ghanimah, not part of the fay'. Because of this question, the commentators mention here two answers:

The first: This verse was not revealed concerning the villages of the Banu al-Nadir, because they were not spurred toward with horses and camels, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the Muslims did not besiege them. Rather, it concerns Fadak, because the people of Fadak withdrew from it, so those villages and property came into the hand of the Messenger (ʿalayhi al-salām) without war. The Messenger (ʿalayhi al-ṣalāt wal-salām) used to take from the income of Fadak his own sustenance and the sustenance of those he supported, and he put the remainder into weapons and horses. When he died, Fatimah (ʿalayha al-salām) claimed that he had granted Fadak to her. Abu Bakr said: "You are the most dear of people to me in poverty and the most beloved to me in wealth, but I do not know the validity of your claim, and it is not permissible for me to rule on that." Then Umm Ayman and a freedman of the Messenger (ʿalayhi al-salām) bore witness for her. Abu Bakr asked her for the witness whose testimony is acceptable in the Sharia, and there was none. So Abu Bakr applied to it what the Messenger (ﷺ) used to apply: he spent from it on those whom the Messenger used to support, and he put what remained into weapons and horses. Likewise 'Umar placed it in the hand of 'Ali to administer it in this manner, and at the end of 'Umar's time he returned it to 'Umar, and said: "We have sufficiency, and the Muslims have need of it." 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him) administered it in the same way, then it passed to 'Ali, and he administered it in this manner. So the four imams agreed upon this.

The second opinion: This verse was revealed concerning the Banu al-Nadir and their villages. The Muslims at that time did not have many horses or camels, and they had not traveled a great distance to them. They were only two miles from Medina, so they walked to them on foot, and none rode except the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who was riding a camel. When the fighting force was small, and the horses and riding camels were not available, God the Exalted treated them as what no fighting force had been involved in at all. So God singled out the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for those properties. Then it is reported that he divided them among the Emigrants, and he gave none of them to the Helpers except three men who were in need: Abu Dujanah, Sahl ibn Hunayf, and al-Harith ibn al-Simmah.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 59, verse 9:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿For the poor emigrants (muhajirun) who were driven out of their homes and their possessions, seeking bounty from God and good pleasure, and who help God and His Messenger. Those are the truthful.﴾

Know that this is a substitute (badal) for His saying: ﴿and to the kinsman, the orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer﴾. It is as if it were said: "By those four, I mean these poor emigrants, who have such-and-such attributes." Then God, exalted is He, described them with several qualities:

The first: they are poor.

The second: they are emigrants.

The third: they were driven out of their homes and their possessions, meaning that the disbelievers of Makkah compelled them to leave, so they are the ones who expelled them.

The fourth: they seek bounty from God and good pleasure. By "bounty" is meant the reward of Paradise, and by "good pleasure" is meant His saying: ﴿And the good pleasure of God is greater﴾ [al-Tawbah: 72].

The fifth: His saying: ﴿and they help God and His Messenger﴾, that is, with their selves and their wealth.

The sixth: His saying: ﴿Those are the truthful﴾, meaning that when they forsook the pleasures of this world and bore its hardships for the sake of the religion, their truthfulness in their religion became manifest. Some scholars have used this verse as evidence for the imamate (leadership) of Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him. He said: These poor ones among the emigrants and the Helpers used to say to Abu Bakr: "O Successor of the Messenger of God!" And God bears witness to their being truthful. So it is necessary that they were truthful in their saying: "O Successor of the Messenger of God!" And when this is the case, it is necessary to affirm with certainty the validity of his imamate.

Then God mentioned the Helpers (Ansar) and praised them, when their souls were content to give up the spoils (fay'), since they were for the emigrants alone, to the exclusion of them. He said:

﴿And those who had settled in the abode and in faith before them love those who emigrate to them, and do not find in their hearts any need for what they have been given, and prefer them above themselves, even though they themselves are in need. And whoever is saved from the stinginess of his own soul, those are the successful.﴾

By "the abode" is meant Madinah, which is the abode of the Hijrah. The Ansar settled in it before the emigrants. The sense of the verse is: "And those who settled in Madinah and in faith before them." (Here) two objections are raised concerning the verse:

The first: it is not said "he settled in faith" (tabawwa'a al-iman).

The second: even granting that such a phrase is used, the Ansar did not settle in faith before the emigrants.

(As for the answer) to the first, there are several aspects:

One: they settled in the abode and made their faith pure, as in the saying of the poet:

*"Indeed I saw you in the battle, wearing a sword and a spear."*

Two: they made faith a firm and settled homeland for themselves, because of their firm attachment to it and their steadfastness upon it, just as, when they asked Salman about his lineage, he said: "I am the son of Islam."

Three: He named Madinah with faith, because faith became manifest and strong in it.

(As for the answer) to the second objection, there are two aspects:

The first: the speech contains inversion (taqdim and ta'khir), and the sense is: "And those who settled in the abode before them, and in faith."

The second: it is by way of omitting a word (hadhf al-mudaf), and the sense is: "They settled in the abode and in faith before the time of their Hijrah."

* * *

Then he said: ﴿and do not find in their hearts any need for what they have been given﴾. Al-Hasan said: that is, envy, burning, and rage at what the emigrants were given in preference to them. The word "need" (hajah) was applied to envy, rage, and burning because these things do not separate from need, so the name of the necessary concomitant was applied to what it necessitates, by way of metonymy (kinayah). Then He said: ﴿and prefer them above themselves, even though they themselves are in need﴾. It is said: "he preferred him with such-and-such" when he gave him preference over himself with it. The object of "preferring" is omitted, and the sense is: "and they prefer them with their wealth and their dwellings over themselves."

From Ibn 'Abbas: "The Prophet (ﷺ) said to the Ansar: 'If you wish, you may divide your houses and your wealth among the emigrants, and I will divide for you from the spoils as I divide for them; and if you wish, the spoils will be for them, and your houses and your wealth will be yours.' They said: 'No; rather we will divide for them from our houses and our wealth, and we will not share with them in the spoils.' So God, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿and prefer them above themselves, even though they themselves are in need﴾."

He thus clarified that this preference was not out of wealth-sufficiency, but out of need and want (khasasah), which is poverty. Its root is from al-khasas, which means gaps (furaj), and every opening in a sieve, a door, a cloud, or a veil is called khasas; its singular is khasasah. The commentators mentioned several kinds of the Ansar's preference for the guest with food, and their making excuses for themselves until the guest was satisfied. Then they mentioned that the verse was revealed concerning that preference. The correct view is that it was revealed because of their preferring the emigrants in the matter of the fay'. Then there is nothing to prevent the rest of preference from entering into it.

Then He said: ﴿And whoever is saved from the stinginess of his own soul, those are the successful.﴾ Shuhh (stinginess) is with a damma or a kasra, and both have been read.

Know that the difference between shuhh and bukhl (miserliness) is that bukhl is the act of withholding itself, while shuhh is the inner state that calls for that withholding. Since shuhh is one of the attributes of the soul, for this reason God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever is saved from the stinginess of his own soul, those are the successful﴾, the ones who attain what they sought. Ibn Zayd said: Whoever does not take what God has forbidden him to take, and does not withhold what God has commanded him to give, has been saved from the stinginess of his soul.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 59, verse 10:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who came after them say, "Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith, and do not put in our hearts any resentment toward those who have believed. Our Lord, indeed You are Compassionate and Merciful."﴾

Know that His saying ﴿And those who came after them﴾ is also a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun), meaning those who emigrated after them. It has also been said: they are the Successors who follow with excellence (al-Tabiʿun bi-ihsan), meaning those who come after the Emigrants and the Helpers (al-Ansar) until the Day of Resurrection. God, exalted is He, mentioned that they supplicate for themselves and for those who preceded them in faith, and that is His saying: ﴿say, "Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith, and do not put in our hearts any resentment toward those who have believed."﴾ That is, ghill (resentment) means deceit, envy and hatred.

Know that these verses have encompassed all the believers, for they are either the Emigrants, or the Helpers, or those who came after them. He made clear that it is among the characteristics of those who came after the Emigrants and the Helpers to mention the foremost ones, who are the Emigrants and the Helpers, with supplication and mercy. Whoever is not like this, but rather mentions them with evil, is outside the categories of the believers according to the text of this verse.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 59, verse 11:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you not considered those who have practiced hypocrisy saying to their brothers who have disbelieved among the People of the Scripture, "If you are expelled, we will surely go out with you, and we will never obey anyone against you, and if you are fought, we will surely support you." And Allah testifies that they are liars.﴾ Al-Muqatil said: he means ʿAbdullah ibn Ubayy, ʿAbdullah ibn Nabtal, and Rifaʿah ibn Zayd. They were from the Ansar, but they practiced hypocrisy, saying to their brothers. This brotherhood admits of several meanings:

The first: brotherhood in disbelief, because the Jews and the hypocrites were joined in general disbelief in Muhammad (ﷺ).

The second: brotherhood by way of friendship, allegiance and mutual assistance.

The third: brotherhood by way of their shared enmity toward Muhammad (ﷺ). Then Allah, exalted is He, informed about them that they said to the Jews: ﴿If you are expelled﴾ from Medina, ﴿we will surely go out with you, and we will never obey anyone against you﴾, that is, in forsaking you, ﴿anyone, ever﴾. They also promised them support by their saying: ﴿And if you are fought, we will surely support you.﴾ Then Allah, exalted is He, bore witness to their being liars in this statement, so He said: ﴿And Allah testifies that they are liars.﴾

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 59, verses 12–13:

When He had testified to their lying in general terms, He followed it with detail, saying: ﴿If they are expelled, they will not go out with them; and if they are fought, they will not help them; and if they help them, they will surely turn their backs; then they will not be helped.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, has knowledge of all the objects of knowledge, which have no end. He knows the existents in the three times (past, present and future), and the non-existents in the three times, and He knows, in each of these six aspects, what would have been the case had things been contrary to what actually happened, and how it would have been under that assumption. Here, God, exalted is He, informed that these Jews, if they were expelled, these hypocrites would not go out with them. And so it was: when the Banu al-Nadir were expelled, the hypocrites did not go out with them, and when they were fought, they did not help them either. As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and if they help them﴾, its meaning is like what a critic who objects to another's speech says: "We do not grant that the matter is as you say; and even if we grant that the matter is as you say, it does not benefit you at all." Likewise here, He, exalted is He, mentioned that they do not help them, and on the assumption that they do help them, they will inevitably abandon that help and be defeated, and leave those whom they helped in the hands of the enemies. The parallel of this verse is His saying: ﴿Had God known any good in them, He would have made them hear; and if He had made them hear, they would have turned away while being averse﴾ [al-Anfal: 23]. As for His saying: ﴿then they will not be helped﴾, there are two possible readings:

The first: it refers to the hypocrites, meaning: the hypocrites will be defeated, then they will not be helped after that, i.e., God will destroy them, and their hypocrisy will not benefit them because their disbelief has become manifest.

The second: the Jews will be defeated, then the help of the hypocrites will not benefit them.

Then God, exalted is He, mentioned that the fear of the hypocrites of the believers is greater than their fear of God, exalted is He, so He said:

﴿Indeed, you are more fearsome in their breasts than God. That is because they are a people who do not understand﴾, i.e., they do not know the greatness of God so that they would fear Him as He deserves to be feared.

* * *

He means that these Jews and hypocrites are not able to fight you collectively except when they are in towns fortified with trenches and fortifications, or from behind walls. This is because God cast terror into their hearts, and because the support and help of God is with you. It is read (judur) with the light vowel (takhfif), and (jidarin), and (jadarin) and (jadrin), and they all mean the wall.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Their might is severe among themselves. You think them united, but their hearts are divided. That is because they are a people who do not understand.﴾ On this verse there are three interpretations:

The first: It means that the severe might for which they are described exists only when some of them are with others. But when they fight you, that might and strength will no longer be theirs, because the brave becomes a coward and the mighty becomes humbled when confronting God and His Messenger.

The second: Mujahid said: The meaning is that when they gather, they say, "We will do such-and-such," and so they threaten the believers with severe might from behind their walls and fortresses. Then they hold back from going out to fight. So their might is severe among themselves, not between themselves and the believers.

The third: Ibn Abbas said: Its meaning is that some of them are enemies to others. **Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 59, verses 21–22:**

﴿The people of the Fire and the people of Paradise are not equal. The people of Paradise are the ones who are successful.﴾

Know that the difference between these two groups is known by necessity. The purpose of mentioning this distinction in such a context is to draw attention to the greatness of that difference. There are two issues here.

The first issue: The Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school) argued that the one who commits a major sin (kabirah) will not enter Paradise, because the verse indicates that the people of the Fire and the people of Paradise are not equal. So if the one who commits a major sin entered Paradise, the people of the Fire and the people of Paradise would be equal, and this is impermissible. Its answer is known.

The second issue: Our companions (the Ash'arites) used this verse to argue that a Muslim is not executed for killing a dhimmi (a non-Muslim under protection). We have explained its reasoning in the *Khilafiyyat* (a work on disputed juristic questions).

Then, when He, exalted is He, had explained these proofs, He magnified the matter of the Qur'an, so He said:

As for His saying: ﴿as-Salam (the Source of Peace)﴾, there are two views:

The first: it means *as-salamah* (safety, freedom from defect), and from it comes *Dar as-Salam* (the Abode of Peace) and *Salamun 'alaykum* (Peace be upon you). He is described by it as an intensification of His being free from deficiencies, just as one says *raja'* (hope), *ghiyath* (help), and *'adl* (justice). If it is asked: according to this interpretation, there is no difference between *al-Quddus* and *as-Salam*, and repetition goes against the original principle?

We say: His being *Quddus* indicates His freedom from all defects in the past and the present, and His being *Salam* indicates that no defect will befall Him in the future, for whatever is subject to defects loses its safety and does not remain safe.

The second: He is *Salam* in the sense that He is the one who causes safety.

As for His saying: ﴿al-Mu'min (the Granter of Security)﴾, there are two views:

The first: He is the one who grants His friends security from His punishment. It is said: *amanahu yu'ammihi*, so he is *mu'min*.

The second: He is the one who confirms the truth (*al-musaddiq*). This is either in the sense that He confirms His prophets by manifesting miracles for them, or because the community of Muhammad ﷺ bear witness for the rest of the prophets, as He said: ﴿that you may be witnesses over mankind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. Then Allah confirms them in that testimony. It was also read with a *fatha* on the *mim* (*al-Mu'mana*), meaning the one in whom one believes, by omitting the preposition, as it was omitted in His saying: ﴿and Musa chose his people﴾ [al-A'raf: 155].

As for His saying: ﴿al-Muhaymin (the Guardian)﴾, they said: its meaning is the witness from whom nothing is hidden. Then there are two views regarding its root. Al-Khalil and Abu 'Ubaydah said: *hayman*, *yuhayminu*, so he is *muhaymin*, when he is watchful over something.

Others said: *muhaymin* originally is *mu'aymin*, from *amana, yu'minu*, so it means *mu'min*. Its full discussion has already passed at His saying: ﴿and a guardian over it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48]. Ibn al-Anbari said: *al-Muhaymin* is the one who maintains His creation by providing for them, and he recited:

*Indeed, the best of people after their Prophet is his guardian, the one who follows him in what is known and what is denied.*

He said: its meaning is the one who maintains the people after him.

As for ﴿al-'Aziz (the Mighty)﴾, it means either the one for whom there is no equal, or the Overpowering, the Subduer.

As for ﴿al-Jabbar (the Compeller)﴾, there are several views:

The first: it is *fa''al* from *jabara*, when He enriches the poor and mends the broken. Al-Azhari said: by my life, He is the one who mends every broken and poor one, and He is the one who mends His religion which He has approved. Al-'Ajjaj said:

*God has mended the religion, so He has mended it.*

The second: *al-Jabbar* is from *jabarahu 'ala kadha*, when he compels him to do what he wants. Al-Suddi said: it is the one who overpowers people and compels them to what He wills. Al-Azhari said: this is the dialect of Tamim, and many of the Hijazis also say it. Al-Shafi'i used to say: *jabarahu al-sultan 'ala kadha* without an *alif* (i.e., *jabara*, not *ajbara*). Al-Farra' took *al-Jabbar* in this sense from *ajbara*, which is the well-known form for compulsion, and he said: I have not heard *fa''al* from *af'ala* except in two words: *jabbar* from *ajbara*, and *darrak* from *adraka*. According to this view, *al-Jabbar* is *al-Qahhar* (the Subduer).

The third: Ibn al-Anbari said: *al-Jabbar* as an attribute of Allah is the one who cannot be reached, and from it comes the saying about the palm tree that escapes the hand of one who reaches for it: *jabbarah*.

The fourth: Ibn 'Abbas said: *al-Jabbar* is the Great King. Al-Wahidi said: what we have mentioned of the meanings of *al-Jabbar* as an attribute of Allah is so. *Al-Jabbar* also has meanings as an attribute of created beings:

First: the one who is empowered, as in His saying: ﴿and you are not over them a compeller﴾ [Qaf: 45].

Second: the one of great physical size, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, therein is a people of great stature﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 22].

Third: the one who rebels against the worship of Allah, as in His saying: ﴿and He has not made me a rebellious tyrant﴾ [Maryam: 32].

Fourth: the one who fights, as in His saying: ﴿you attacked as tyrants﴾, and His saying: ﴿You only want to be a tyrant in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 19].

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 59, verses 21–22:**

﴿The people of the Fire and the people of Paradise are not equal. The people of Paradise are the ones who are successful.﴾

Know that the difference between these two groups is known by necessity. The purpose of mentioning this distinction in such a context is to draw attention to the greatness of that difference. There are two issues here.

The first issue: The Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school) argued that the one who commits a major sin (kabirah) will not enter Paradise, because the verse indicates that the people of the Fire and the people of Paradise are not equal. So if the one who commits a major sin entered Paradise, the people of the Fire and the people of Paradise would be equal, and this is impermissible. Its answer is known.

The second issue: Our companions (the Ash'arites) used this verse to argue that a Muslim is not executed for killing a dhimmi (a non-Muslim under protection). We have explained its reasoning in the *Khilafiyyat* (a work on disputed juristic questions).

Then, when He, exalted is He, had explained these proofs, He magnified the matter of the Qur'an, so He said:

﴿Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled and split apart from fear of Allah.﴾ The meaning is that if a mind had been placed in the mountain as it has been placed in you, and then the Qur'an had been sent down upon it, it would have submitted, humbled itself, and split apart from fear of Allah.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And these are the parables We set forth for the people, that they may reflect.﴾ That is, the purpose of mentioning this statement is to draw attention to the hardness of the hearts of these disbelievers and the coarseness of their natures. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Then your hearts became hard after that, so they were like stones or even harder in hardness.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 74]

Know that when He described the Qur'an as great, and it is known that the greatness of the attribute follows the greatness of the one described, He followed that with an explanation of the greatness of Allah, so He said:

﴿He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed. He is the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.﴾ It has been said: "the secret and the open," and it has been said: "this world and the Hereafter."

Know that He, exalted is He, placed *al-ghayb* (the unseen) before *al-shahadah* (the witnessed) in the wording, and there is a rational secret in this. As for the exegetes, they mentioned several views on *al-ghayb* and *al-shahadah*. It has been said: *al-ghayb* is what is non-existent, and *al-shahadah* is what exists; or *al-ghayb* is what is hidden from the servants, and *al-shahadah* is what they have witnessed.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, the King﴾. All of this has already been explained.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿al-Quddus (the Holy One)﴾. It has been read with a *damm* (*al-Qudduus*) and with a *fatha* (*al-Qaddus*). It means the one who is most absolutely free from imperfection in His essence, attributes, actions, rulings, and names. We explained it at the beginning of Surah al-Hadid, and some of it passed in the explanation of His saying: ﴿and we glorify You﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. Al-Hasan said: it is the One whose blessings are abundant.

As for His saying: ﴿as-Salam (the Source of Peace)﴾, there are two views:

The first: it means *as-salamah* (safety, freedom from defect), and from it comes *Dar as-Salam* (the Abode of Peace) and *Salamun 'alaykum* (Peace be upon you). He is described by it as an intensification of His being free from deficiencies, just as one says *raja'* (hope), *ghiyath* (help), and *'adl* (justice). If it is asked: according to this interpretation, there is no difference between *al-Quddus* and *as-Salam*, and repetition goes against the original principle?

We say: His being *Quddus* indicates His freedom from all defects in the past and the present, and His being *Salam* indicates that no defect will befall Him in the future, for whatever is subject to defects loses its safety and does not remain safe.

The second: He is *Salam* in the sense that He is the one who causes safety.

As for His saying: ﴿al-Mu'min (the Granter of Security)﴾, there are two views:

The first: He is the one who grants His friends security from His punishment. It is said: *amanahu yu'ammihi*, so he is *mu'min*.

The second: He is the one who confirms the truth (*al-musaddiq*). This is either in the sense that He confirms His prophets by manifesting miracles for them, or because the community of Muhammad ﷺ bear witness for the rest of the prophets, as He said: ﴿that you may be witnesses over mankind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. Then Allah confirms them in that testimony. It was also read with a *fatha* on the *mim* (*al-Mu'mana*), meaning the one in whom one believes, by omitting the preposition, as it was omitted in His saying: ﴿and Musa chose his people﴾ [al-A'raf: 155].

As for His saying: ﴿al-Muhaymin (the Guardian)﴾, they said: its meaning is the witness from whom nothing is hidden. Then there are two views regarding its root. Al-Khalil and Abu 'Ubaydah said: *hayman*, *yuhayminu*, so he is *muhaymin*, when he is watchful over something.

Others said: *muhaymin* originally is *mu'aymin*, from *amana, yu'minu*, so it means *mu'min*. Its full discussion has already passed at His saying: ﴿and a guardian over it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48]. Ibn al-Anbari said: *al-Muhaymin* is the one who maintains His creation by providing for them, and he recited:

*Indeed, the best of people after their Prophet is his guardian, the one who follows him in what is known and what is denied.*

He said: its meaning is the one who maintains the people after him.

As for ﴿al-'Aziz (the Mighty)﴾, it means either the one for whom there is no equal, or the Overpowering, the Subduer.

As for ﴿al-Jabbar (the Compeller)﴾, there are several views:

The first: it is *fa''al* from *jabara*, when He enriches the poor and mends the broken. Al-Azhari said: by my life, He is the one who mends every broken and poor one, and He is the one who mends His religion which He has approved. Al-'Ajjaj said:

*God has mended the religion, so He has mended it.*

The second: *al-Jabbar* is from *jabarahu 'ala kadha*, when he compels him to do what he wants. Al-Suddi said: it is the one who overpowers people and compels them to what He wills. Al-Azhari said: this is the dialect of Tamim, and many of the Hijazis also say it. Al-Shafi'i used to say: *jabarahu al-sultan 'ala kadha* without an *alif* (i.e., *jabara*, not *ajbara*). Al-Farra' took *al-Jabbar* in this sense from *ajbara*, which is the well-known form for compulsion, and he said: I have not heard *fa''al* from *af'ala* except in two words: *jabbar* from *ajbara*, and *darrak* from *adraka*. According to this view, *al-Jabbar* is *al-Qahhar* (the Subduer).

The third: Ibn al-Anbari said: *al-Jabbar* as an attribute of Allah is the one who cannot be reached, and from it comes the saying about the palm tree that escapes the hand of one who reaches for it: *jabbarah*.

The fourth: Ibn 'Abbas said: *al-Jabbar* is the Great King. Al-Wahidi said: what we have mentioned of the meanings of *al-Jabbar* as an attribute of Allah is so. *Al-Jabbar* also has meanings as an attribute of created beings:

First: the one who is empowered, as in His saying: ﴿and you are not over them a compeller﴾ [Qaf: 45].

Second: the one of great physical size, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, therein is a people of great stature﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 22].

Third: the one who rebels against the worship of Allah, as in His saying: ﴿and He has not made me a rebellious tyrant﴾ [Maryam: 32].

Fourth: the one who fights, as in His saying: ﴿you attacked as tyrants﴾, and His saying: ﴿You only want to be a tyrant in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 19].

Regarding His saying, ﴿The Compeller (al-Mutakabbir)﴾, there are several opinions:

First: Ibn ʿAbbas said: He who is magnified in His lordship, so there is nothing like Him.

Second: Qatadah said: The one who is exalted above every evil.

Third: al-Zajjaj said: The one who is exalted above wronging the servants.

Fourth: Ibn al-Anbari said: al-Mutakabbir is the Possessor of greatness (al-kibriya'), and kibriya' among the Arabs means sovereignty (al-mulk). From this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and that you two may have greatness (al-kibriya') in the land﴾ [Yunus: 78].

Know that al-mutakabbir, when applied to created beings, is a term of blame, because the one who is mutakabbir is the one who displays greatness from himself, and that is a deficiency with respect to created beings, for he has no greatness or loftiness; rather, with him there is nothing but lowliness, humiliation and neediness. So when he displays loftiness he is a liar, and this is blameworthy in his case. As for the Real, glory be to Him, all kinds of loftiness and greatness belong to Him. So when He displays it, He has guided the servants to recognize His majesty and His loftiness, and this is the utmost praise in His regard, glory be to Him. For this reason, when He mentioned this name He said: ﴿Glory be to Allah above what they associate with Him﴾, as if it were said: Created beings may act with arrogance and claim to share with Allah in this attribute, but He, glory be to Him, is exalted above the greatness that is found in created beings, because they are deficient by their very essences, so their claim to greatness adds the deficiency of falsehood to their inherent deficiency. As for the Real, glory be to Him, He possesses loftiness and might, so when He displays it, that is the addition of perfection to perfection. So glory be to Allah above what they associate with Him in ascribing the attribute of being mutakabbir to created beings.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿He is Allah, the Creator (al-Khaliq)﴾. Khalq is taqdir (measuring/determining). Its meaning is that He determines His acts in specific ways, so the attribute of being Creator returns to the attribute of will (al-irada).

* * *

Then He said: ﴿the Originator (al-Bari')﴾, which is equivalent to our saying: ṣani' (maker) and mujid (bringer into existence), except that it indicates the innovation (ikhtira') of bodies. For this reason one says of created beings: bariyyah, but one does not say it of accidents such as color and taste.

As for al-Musawwir (the Fashioner): its meaning is that He creates the forms of creatures as He wills. He mentioned al-Khaliq before al-Bari' because the preponderance of will precedes the effect of power. And He placed al-Bari' before al-Musawwir because the bringing into existence of essences precedes the bringing into existence of attributes.
